segments.original: The first critics and commentators to take popular cinema seriously tended to value the so-called "golden age" of the Hollywood studios in the 1930s and 1940s, somewhat arbitrarily labeling 1939 as "the greatest year in film." segments.original: "Someday a real rain will come and wash all this scum off the streets". So mutters tormented cab driver Travis Bickle, played with almost furious intensity by Robert De Niro, in the first of his acclaimed leading roles in Martin Scorsese's films. Bickle's job, crisscrossing New York from one end to the other ("anytime, anywhere"), gives him a sleepless view of the city's underbelly, everything that happens in the dark alleys that most people never witness. He ends up so accustomed to the world around him, however, that he feels numb, invisible and, ultimately, powerless.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Taxi Driver's portraits of urban disorder and malaise are as dark and claustrophobic as they come. The film has some elements of film noir (Bickle's voice-over narration, the jazzy score by Bernard Herrmann (1911-1975)) but departs radically from the pattern when it comes to storytelling. Taxi Driver unfolds like a noir told from the perspective of an anonymous stranger standing in front of a murder scene, peering over the police cordon to see the covered body in the street. What is this person thinking? How would they react when confronted with such vivid exposure to violence?

segments.original: Scorsese, Schrader and De Niro seem to be asking viewers the same thing. Throughout the film, we are forced to observe the city from Bickle's relentlessly isolated perspective, with only a few glimmers of hope carrying us outside his maladjusted mind. He is Dostoevsky's "underground man", who emerges with a gun and a death wish, an antihero who takes justice into his own hands, taking a hands-on approach to cleaning up the city. "Here is a man who won't take it anymore," he announces triumphantly. "A man who stood up against the scum, the sluts, the dogs, the filth, the shit. Here is a man who stood up."

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Based on the bestseller by Ken Kesey, written after his experience working at a veterans' hospital in California, the film is set in a state mental institution where the wily nonconformist Randle P. McMurphy (Jack Nicholson) is committed for rehabilitation. Inside the institution, he is kept under the watchful eye of the sadistic Nurse Ratched (Louise Fletcher, in a role turned down by several major Hollywood actresses, including Jane Fonda, Anne Bancroft, Ellen Burstyn, and Faye Dunaway), and he soon stages a rebellion against her with the help of other patients.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A groundbreaking film that Kesey reportedly never wanted to see (he was supposedly irritated that the story was not told from the point of view of Chief Bromden (Will Sampson), as in his book), One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest became part of Oscar history when it became only the second film up to that time to win all five major awards. Each one was deserved: Czech director Milos Forman (1932-2018) created a hypnotic, humanistic film full of eccentric characters (among the actors who made their film debuts are Brad Dourif (b. 1950) and Christopher Lloyd (b. 1938)), and drew one of the best performances of Fletcher's career. Nicholson, naturally, is captivating as McMurphy, imprisoned yet witty and full of life, and the scenes in which he faces off with the despicable Nurse Ratched are the most electrifying in this modern classic of American cinema.
